title: The late Indian masters
hookLine: Vikramashila and the teachers who later carried Buddhism to Tibet

cards: A request arrives at a monastery in eastern India. It comes from the north, from Tibet, and it asks for one teacher by name.

The Tibetan histories tell it as a long courtship: messengers, gifts of gold, a refusal, then a second try. The teacher they wanted was a senior monk at the monastery of Vikramashila, known in Tibet as Atisha.

His own monastery did not want to give him up, and tradition says it let him go only for a time, expecting him back. In the end he went, crossed the mountains, and taught in Tibet until he died there.

teach.b: First, the place. Vikramashila stood in eastern India, a monastery that tradition says was founded and supported by kings.

Like Nalanda, it was a place of study: monks trained in philosophy, debate, meditation and ritual, and its leading teachers were honored by name. Second, the man. Atisha's monastic name was Dipankara Shrijnana.
Tradition says he studied with many teachers, in India and, by some accounts, across the sea in a land called Suvarnadvipa, the golden island. Third, the book.
In Tibet, Atisha wrote a short work called the Lamp for the Path to Awakening.

teach.h: THE LAMP: THREE KINDS OF PEOPLE.
teach.b: It sorts practitioners into three kinds of people: those who seek a better life to come, those who seek their own freedom, and those who seek awakening for the sake of all beings.
Each stage, it says, rests on the one before, the way a second floor rests on a first.

Tibetan teachers later built long teachings on the stages of the path on that frame, and his close Tibetan student, Dromtonpa, gathered his followers into the Kadampa tradition. Fourth, the thread. Atisha was not alone.

In these generations Indian teachers traveled north and Tibetan translators traveled south to study, and the learning of the Indian monasteries crossed the mountains in their heads and in their luggage.

teach.h: TEACHER TO STUDENT, NAME BY NAME.
teach.b: Tibetan lineages still keep the names, teacher to student, back to the halls of India.
Behind a teaching given in Tibet today stands a chain of people, and some of the links were monks at Vikramashila.

how: In Tibetan Buddhism a teaching is usually received through a lineage, and students often learn the names of the teachers who handed it down; Atisha's three kinds of people still frame Tibetan teachings on the stages of the path.

games.q: you lead the monastery of Vikramashila. messengers from Tibet ask for your senior teacher. what do you do?
o: let him go, but ask that he come back.
games.why: the Tibetan accounts say the monastery let him go only for a time and expected him back. he stayed in Tibet for the rest of his life.

practice: Bring to mind someone who taught you something that mattered, a parent, a coach, a friend, an old boss, then step back one link: who taught them?
A grandmother, a mentor, a book they loved; hold that person in mind for a few breaths. If you pray, you can thank them in your own way, and if not, simply let the thanks travel back along the chain.
